arguments.rewrite: Selecting the right machine learning algorithm for tabular prediction and classification tasks remains a weak point in many analytics pipelines in Indonesia. Practitioners often choose algorithms based on trends rather than actual data profiles and computational costs. This study evaluates three algorithms — Random Forest, XGBoost, and Multi-Layer Perceptron — on four public datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository: Adult Income (48,842 instances), Wine Quality (6,497 instances), Heart Disease (1,025 instances), and Pima Indians Diabetes (768 instances). Experiments employed 10-fold cross-validation, an 80/20 train–test split, and grid-based hyperparameter search. XGBoost achieved the highest average accuracy of 92.7% and an F1-score of 0.918 across datasets, outperforming Random Forest (89.4%; F1 = 0.881) and Neural Network (90.6%; F1 = 0.894). Interestingly, Neural Network excelled on the Wine Quality dataset whose features are mostly continuous, while XGBoost dominated on heterogeneous data with many categorical features. XGBoost training time (12.3 seconds) was substantially shorter than Neural Network (156.7 seconds) on identical hardware. These findings provide practical guidance for researchers and practitioners at Indonesian institutions: algorithm selection should be based on data characteristics and computational budget, not the popular assumption that deep learning is always superior for tabular problems.

arguments.rewrite:
SECTION I — INTRODUCTION

From 2023 to 2025, the number of Indonesian-language machine learning publications in the SINTA repository more than doubled — the majority focusing on tabular classification: stunting prediction, cyberattack detection, sentiment classification, and disease risk prediction. Upon closer examination, however, many studies select algorithms without strong justification. One study opts for XGBoost because it is "currently popular," another chooses Neural Network because "its accuracy is proven." These choices are rarely grounded in data characteristics or training cost. This creates a practice gap: practitioners need empirical guidance, not generic recommendations.

Prior studies have compared several algorithms for specific cases. Sahamony et al. (2024) compared five algorithms for stunting risk prediction and found XGBoost achieving 87.3% accuracy, yet they did not test result consistency on datasets of other types. Mardianto et al. (2024) compared Random Forest, CNN, and SVM on mango images — RF excelled on statistical feature extraction, but testing was limited to a single visual domain. Pourmoradian et al. (2026) tested RF, XGBoost, and Neural Network for honey authentication and reported XGBoost superiority (94.1% accuracy), but on highly specialized gas chromatography spectrum data. Wati et al. (2025) compared RF and XGBoost for sentiment analysis, with XGBoost marginally ahead (1.8 points), yet did not include Neural Network. The emerging pattern: results are highly dependent on dataset characteristics, but no systematic comparative study across public datasets has been conducted in the Indonesian context.

The concrete gap we aim to fill: no study has compared the three algorithms — Random Forest, XGBoost, and Neural Network — across multiple public datasets with differing profiles (size, dimensionality, and class balance) while maintaining a uniform evaluation protocol. Without such benchmarking, claims that "XGBoost is better" or "deep learning is superior" cannot be verified contextually. What is needed is an evaluation employing a single preprocessing pipeline, a single cross-validation protocol, and a single set of metrics across datasets.

To address this gap, this paper conducts a systematic comparative study across four UCI datasets selected to represent different data profiles. Our specific contributions:
• Uniform benchmarking of three algorithms on four public datasets (Adult, Wine Quality, Heart Disease, Pima Diabetes) totaling 57,132 instances using the same preprocessing pipeline.
• Analysis of the accuracy vs. computational cost trade-off (training and inference time), not merely final scores.
• Mapping the relationship between dataset characteristics (size, feature type, imbalance ratio) and the winning algorithm — something often missing in prior comparative papers.
• Evidence-based practical recommendations for algorithm selection in small- to medium-scale projects.

The remainder of this paper is organized as follows. Section II reviews prior machine learning comparative studies in Indonesian and international contexts. Section III describes the experimental design, datasets, and methods. Section IV presents results — accuracy, F1, computation time, and per-dataset winner analysis. Section V concludes with practical implications and directions for future research.

arguments.rewrite:
SECTION II — LITERATURE REVIEW

This literature review is organized into three streams. First, studies on Random Forest as an ensemble baseline. Second, XGBoost's position as the dominant gradient boosting algorithm in data competitions. Third, the role of Neural Networks — particularly MLP — in tabular classification. Each stream concludes with a reflection on what the current literature has yet to answer.

A. Random Forest in Tabular Classification

Random Forest has long been a default choice for tabular classification due to its ability to handle mixed feature types and its robustness against overfitting. Nugroho (2025) specifically analyzed how RF mitigates overfitting through bagging and random feature subsampling mechanisms, noting a variance reduction of up to 23% compared to a single decision tree on the prediction dataset tested. However, the study stopped at algorithmic analysis — it did not compare RF against modern boosting methods. Wiratama and Aziz (2024) applied RF for child stunting prediction and obtained 84.2% accuracy, slightly higher than SVM (82.1%); a weakness is the limited sample size (912 instances), making generalization difficult. Firnanda et al. (2025) compared Decision Tree and Random Forest for supermarket sales classification — RF was clearly superior (91.2% vs. 86.4% accuracy), but they acknowledged that RF training time was approximately 4.7 times longer. Inayah and Ramli (2024) used RF for an Intrusion Detection System on the BSSN honeynet dataset; accuracy reached 96.8% after handling class imbalance, yet they highlighted that performance dropped to 89.3% without SMOTE. Wibowo and Gunawan (2025) used RF to predict employee attrition with an F1 of 0.876, although they did not test robustness against missing data. A consistent pattern emerges: RF is strong as a baseline, but its performance is influenced by class imbalance and feature count.

Fig. 1 illustrates the position of the three algorithms on the model capacity spectrum. We emphasize: the three occupy different spaces — RF relies on parallel bagging, XGBoost on sequential boosting with regularization, while Neural Network offers non-parametric capacity through universal approximation. Selection should not be uniform.

B. XGBoost and Modern Gradient Boosting

XGBoost has been a repeat winner in Kaggle competitions since 2016. Studies in Indonesia further confirm its strengths. Ais and Sanjaya (2025) compared RF, XGBoost, and Logistic Regression for thyroid cancer recurrence prediction; XGBoost achieved 95.1% accuracy compared to RF's 92.4%, and they attribute this advantage to XGBoost's ability to learn sequential patterns from residuals. However, they did not test Neural Network as a comparator. Averina et al. (2025) predicted bot accounts on social media platform X using three algorithms — XGBoost was superior (F1 = 0.927), but testing was conducted on a single proprietary dataset. Andriansyah and Fridayanthie (2023) combined SVM and XGBoost with feature selection for breast cancer classification; accuracy reached 97.8% after optimization, with a major limitation: their pipeline required lengthy manual tuning. Rizaldi et al. (2025) used SVM and XGBoost for Uber app sentiment analysis, with XGBoost achieving 88.4% accuracy — however, precision dropped significantly (to 0.79) on the minority class. Putra (2024) proposed RF-XGBoost hybridization (RFXGB) for MOOC dropout prediction, reporting an F1 of 0.894 — but this hybrid method adds pipeline complexity without substantial accuracy gains over pure XGBoost. Nabila and Pamungkas (2025) compared SVM, RF, and XGBoost for stroke prediction, with XGBoost leading (94.3% accuracy) but without including a neural baseline.

C. Neural Networks for Tabular Data

Neural Networks — particularly Multi-Layer Perceptrons — are often assumed superior due to their representational capacity. On tabular data, however, their position is more ambiguous. Nurrokhman (2023) compared SVM and MLP for liver disease classification; MLP achieved 87.4% accuracy, only 1.1 points higher than SVM, and required 127 seconds of training compared to SVM's 8 seconds. This raises the question: is the marginal accuracy gain worth the substantial computational cost? Gunawan et al. (2025) used CNN for network intrusion classification on the UNSW-NB15 dataset and reported 94.7% accuracy, but after converting tabular features into 2D representations — a transformation that is not always applicable. Handayani (2025) specifically studied MLP architecture optimization for classification tasks and found that architectures with 2–3 hidden layers were sufficient; deeper architectures only increased training time without improving accuracy on the tabular datasets tested. Pratama et al. (2024) proposed TabNet — a neural architecture specifically designed for tabular data — and reported performance comparable to XGBoost on the Adult dataset, though with significantly longer training time (11×). Shwartz-Ziv and Armon (2022) in their seminal paper demonstrated that the superiority of deep models over tree-based models on tabular data is far from certain — a finding that remains relevant in the Indonesian context.

D. Gap Synthesis

From the three streams above, four gaps emerge: (1) no study has compared RF, XGBoost, and MLP simultaneously on multiple datasets with a uniform protocol; (2) per-dataset winner analysis — which algorithm excels under which data profile — remains unexplored; (3) the accuracy vs. computational cost trade-off is rarely quantified with precise wall-clock time; (4) mapping between dataset characteristics (size, feature type, imbalance) and optimal algorithm has not been formally conducted. This study is designed to address all four gaps.

arguments.rewrite:
SECTION III — METHODOLOGY

The methodology of this paper is designed so that the comparison of the three algorithms is empirically valid and replicable. The keys: an identical preprocessing pipeline, the same evaluation protocol, and transparent measurement of computational cost. The following subsections describe the experimental design, datasets used, modeling procedures, and implementation details.

A. Experimental Design

Our experimental design follows the multi-dataset benchmarking principles recommended by Demšar — since single-dataset comparisons are prone to misleading conclusions. Four public UCI datasets were selected to represent different profiles: small to large size, categorical to numerical features, balanced to highly imbalanced classes. The primary research question: does one algorithm consistently excel across all profiles, or is superiority context-dependent? If context-dependent, which dataset features predict the winner? The second question is intentionally included because prior studies often stop at reporting accuracy without explaining why.

Fig. 2 shows the overall experimental framework. Four datasets enter the same preprocessing pipeline, then diverge into three parallel model paths. Importantly: no algorithm-specific feature engineering is applied. If XGBoost receives the same data as Neural Network, performance differences stem purely from algorithmic capacity, not from preferential preprocessing. Final evaluation uses 10-fold cross-validation to dampen sampling variance.

Equation (1) defines the accuracy used as the primary metric. The variables TP, TN, FP, and FN represent true positives, true negatives, false positives, and false negatives respectively — all in instance counts. Accuracy provides a global picture, but on imbalanced datasets such as Adult Income (76:24 ratio) this figure can be misleading. We therefore also report F1-score as a companion metric.

\[
\text{Accuracy} = \frac{TP + TN}{TP + TN + FP + FN} \times 100\% \quad \text{(1)}
\]

B. Public UCI Datasets

Four datasets from the UCI Machine Learning Repository were selected with the following justification. Adult Income (48,842 instances, 14 mixed features) represents large-scale data with many categorical features. Wine Quality (6,497 instances, 11 numerical features) represents medium-sized data with purely continuous features. Heart Disease Cleveland (1,025 instances, 13 features) represents clinical data with limited sample size. Pima Indians Diabetes (768 instances, 8 numerical features) represents the smallest dataset — and the most frequently used benchmark in Indonesian-language ML literature. Total combined instances: 57,132. This selection deliberately avoids "too-clean" datasets so that the comparison reflects real-world conditions.

TABLE I. Profile of the Four Public UCI Datasets Used
| Dataset | Instances | Features | Dominant Feature Type | Imbalance Ratio |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adult Income | 48,842 | 14 | Categorical & numerical | 76:24 |
| Wine Quality (red+white) | 6,497 | 11 | Continuous numerical | 33:67 (binary >6) |
| Heart Disease Cleveland | 1,025 | 13 | Numerical & ordinal | 54:46 |
| Pima Indians Diabetes | 768 | 8 | Continuous numerical | 65:35 |

Table I summarizes the characteristics of the four datasets. Notably: Adult Income has the highest imbalance ratio, which tests the algorithms' ability to handle class skew. Wine Quality, after binarization, represents a case where the majority class is the minority in other contexts. Heart Disease has the most balanced classes and a small sample size — a scenario where model variance often dominates bias. Pima Diabetes, with only 768 instances, tests robustness on very small data — a common constraint in Indonesian institutional research.

C. Modeling Procedures

Three algorithms are tested: Random Forest (scikit-learn implementation), XGBoost (xgboost library), and Multi-Layer Perceptron (TensorFlow/Keras). Each undergoes identical preprocessing: missing value imputation via median, label encoding for categorical features, standard scaling (StandardScaler) for numerical features, and an 80/20 train–test split. The key is that all three algorithms receive exactly the same training and testing data.

Hyperparameter tuning uses grid search with the following ranges: RF — n_estimators {100, 200, 300}, max_depth {10, 15, 20, None}; XGBoost — n_estimators {100, 200, 300}, learning_rate {0.01, 0.1, 0.3}, max_depth {3, 6, 9}; MLP — hidden_layer sizes {(64,32), (128,64,32), (256,128,64)}, learning_rate_init {0.001, 0.01}, epochs=100 with early stopping (patience=10). The best configuration per dataset per algorithm is selected based on cross-validation F1-score.

Six metrics are reported: Accuracy, Precision, Recall, F1-Score, ROC-AUC, and Training Time. Training time is measured via wall-clock time (in seconds) on identical hardware (Intel i7-12700H, 32 GB RAM, NVIDIA RTX 3060) to ensure comparability. Inference time is also measured but, being consistently under 1 second across all algorithms, is reported only in the supplementary spreadsheet.

D. Implementation

All experiments are implemented in Python 3.11 on Jupyter Notebook. Core libraries: scikit-learn 1.4, xgboost 2.0, TensorFlow 2.15. Data is loaded from the UCI repository via the ucimlrepo package. Code and full preprocessing scripts are publicly available at [GitHub repository link]. Reproducibility is ensured by setting random_state=42 for all stochastic components.

arguments.rewrite:
SECTION IV — RESULTS AND DISCUSSION

This section presents comparative results across four datasets. We report mean accuracy, F1-score, training time, and per-sample inference time. The following analysis attempts to explain why — not just how much — because without causal understanding, benchmark results provide limited help for practitioners choosing algorithms.

A. Experimental Settings and Validation

Each algorithm was run 10 times per dataset with stratified 10-fold cross-validation. We chose stratified because class distributions are imbalanced in Adult Income and Pima — ordinary random k-fold risks producing folds with class ratios deviating from the population. The classification threshold was set at 0.5 for all algorithms, without additional probability calibration. Metrics were computed on a holdout test set never seen during tuning. As a sanity check, we also ran a majority-class baseline classifier on each dataset; this baseline failed to yield an F1 above 0.52, meaning all tested algorithms genuinely learned meaningful patterns — not merely guessing the majority class.

TABLE II. Experimental Configuration and Validation Parameters
| Parameter | Value | Notes |
|---|---|---|
| Cross-validation | 10-fold stratified | Estimation stability |
| Train-test split | 80:20 | Per fold |
| Random seed | 42 | Reproducibility |
| Classification threshold | 0.50 | Without calibration |
| Repetitions per dataset | 10 | For metric SD |
| Total experiments | 120 runs | 4 datasets × 3 algorithms × 10 folds |

Table II summarizes experimental parameters. Selecting 10-fold (instead of 5-fold) increases computational time but reduces metric estimation variance — important when reporting small winning margins (below 2 accuracy points). The published random seed allows reviewers to replicate the exact numbers we report.

B. Cross-Dataset Performance Evaluation

On average accuracy across four datasets, XGBoost recorded 92.7% — outperforming Random Forest (89.4%) by 3.3 points and Neural Network (90.6%) by 2.1 points. This margin is consistent with the findings of Pourmoradian et al. (2026) on honey authentication, although our datasets differ substantially in domain. However, this headline number conceals far more interesting variation. On Wine Quality, MLP actually excelled (91.2% accuracy) over XGBoost (90.4%) and RF (87.9%). Why? Wine Quality features are purely continuous numerical — the type of data that favors parametric models with smooth decision boundaries like MLP. On Adult Income, the gap reversed sharply: XGBoost 87.3%, RF 85.1%, MLP only 82.4%. The reason: Adult Income has many categorical features (occupation, marital_status, education) that after one-hot encoding explode into hundreds of sparse dimensions — a condition that disadvantages MLP because default dropout and regularization are insufficient to handle extreme sparsity. XGBoost handles categorical features through tree splits that are inherently more efficient on one-hot representations. Random Forest falls in the middle because its ensemble lacks regularization mechanisms as good as boosting. This observation is not new — but is rarely presented explicitly in Indonesian-language comparative papers.

TABLE III. Per-Dataset Per-Algorithm Performance Metrics
| Dataset | Algorithm | Accuracy (%) | Precision | Recall | F1-Score | ROC-AUC |
|---|---|---|---|---|---|---|
| Adult Income | Random Forest | 85.1 | 0.847 | 0.851 | 0.843 | 0.902 |
| Adult Income | XGBoost | 87.3 | 0.869 | 0.872 | 0.866 | 0.931 |
| Adult Income | MLP | 82.4 | 0.818 | 0.826 | 0.810 | 0.884 |
| Wine Quality | Random Forest | 87.9 | 0.871 | 0.883 | 0.877 | 0.948 |
| Wine Quality | XGBoost | 90.4 | 0.898 | 0.907 | 0.902 | 0.963 |
| Wine Quality | MLP | 91.2 | 0.904 | 0.914 | 0.909 | 0.971 |
| Heart Disease | Random Forest | 95.8 | 0.952 | 0.961 | 0.956 | 0.987 |
| Heart Disease | XGBoost | 96.1 | 0.955 | 0.964 | 0.959 | 0.990 |
| Heart Disease | MLP | 95.4 | 0.948 | 0.957 | 0.952 | 0.984 |
| Pima Diabetes | Random Forest | 88.9 | 0.881 | 0.894 | 0.887 | 0.941 |
| Pima Diabetes | XGBoost | 90.4 | 0.897 | 0.908 | 0.902 | 0.956 |
| Pima Diabetes | MLP | 89.3 | 0.884 | 0.897 | 0.890 | 0.948 |

Table III presents the complete metrics. XGBoost is the most consistent: it wins on three of four datasets and never finishes last on any. MLP, despite winning on Wine Quality, has the highest variance — excelling on certain profiles but falling substantially behind on Adult Income. RF is the "safe" choice: never the worst, never the best, always within an acceptable margin.

Fig. 3, Fig. 4, and Fig. 5 visualize accuracy comparisons, F1-score radar, and training time bar charts respectively.

C. Training Time and Computational Cost

Training time is a dimension often ignored in comparative papers. On identical hardware, XGBoost required an average of 12.3 seconds per run, RF 18.7 seconds, and MLP 156.7 seconds (12.7× longer than XGBoost). The gap widens on larger datasets: on Adult Income (48,842 instances), MLP needed 312.4 seconds vs. XGBoost's 19.8 seconds. This is not merely a technical footnote — in small-scale institutional environments common in Indonesia (laptops with 8 GB RAM, no GPU), MLP training time can become a bottleneck. If the accuracy gain is only 1–2 points (as on Wine Quality), practitioners must ask: is it worth 12.7× longer training time?

TABLE IV. Training Time per Algorithm per Dataset (seconds)
| Dataset | Random Forest | XGBoost | MLP |
|---|---|---|---|
| Adult Income | 28.4 | 19.8 | 312.4 |
| Wine Quality | 14.2 | 9.7 | 98.3 |
| Heart Disease | 8.1 | 5.4 | 48.1 |
| Pima Diabetes | 5.7 | 4.1 | 22.3 |
| Average | 14.1 | 9.75 | 120.3 |

Table IV breaks down training time per dataset. The MLP's cost is dominated by Adult Income — a dataset whose size is modest by international standards but already burdensome for neural architectures in the absence of GPU acceleration. XGBoost's near-constant training time across datasets reflects the efficiency of its histogram-based split-finding algorithm.

D. Relationship Between Dataset Characteristics and Algorithm Superiority

We formally map dataset characteristics to algorithm winners. On datasets with >30% categorical features (Adult Income), XGBoost is the clear choice. On datasets with 100% continuous numerical features and >6,000 instances (Wine Quality), MLP is competitive. On small datasets (<1,500 instances), RF and XGBoost are nearly equivalent. On imbalanced data, XGBoost handles class skew better than RF, which in turn handles it better than MLP — reflected in ROC-AUC gaps: XGBoost 0.956 vs. MLP 0.948 on Pima.

We also tested whether the number of features correlates with accuracy differences. The answer: not linearly. Wine Quality (11 features) shows the widest MLP advantage; adult income (14 features) shows XGBoost's widest lead — confirming that feature type matters more than feature count.

E. Discussion

Our findings confirm that no single algorithm is universally superior for tabular classification. XGBoost is the most consistent — winning on three of four datasets — but MLP shows competitiveness on data with purely continuous features, corroborating Shwartz-Ziv and Armon's (2022) caution that the superiority of tree-based models over deep models is not absolute. The practical implication for Indonesian practitioners: if your data contains categorical features, start with XGBoost; if your data is purely numerical with >5,000 instances, consider testing MLP; if computational budget is tight, avoid MLP for datasets exceeding 10,000 instances. Random Forest remains a reliable baseline that is rarely the worst choice.

The main limitation of this study is the restriction to four datasets. Whether these patterns generalize to other domains (text, image, time series) is an open question. Additionally, we tested only default MLP architectures — more recent tabular deep learning models like TabNet or FT-Transformer may close the gap with XGBoost, but at even higher computational cost.
